svg.title: Anatomy of an MP-BGP VPNv4 route: the NLRI fields and the attributes that carry policy
svg.desc: A route drawn as a labelled byte strip: eight bytes of route distinguisher, four bytes of IPv4 prefix, and a three-byte label field, followed by the attributes: route targets as an extended community, the next hop which is the PE loopback, the origin and AS path, local preference and MED. Annotations explain each field's job: the RD makes the prefix unique, the IPv4 part is the customer's own prefix unchanged, the label is the VPN label that identifies the destination VRF at the egress, and the route target is the only field that policy acts on. A right panel contrasts what happens at the ingress and egress PE: push at ingress, pop at egress. A closing note warns that the next hop must be reachable through the transport, which is why a broken LSP makes BGP look broken.
svg.text: A VPNv4 route is a prefix plus a label plus a policy tag — nothing more
Read the fields left to right and every L3VPN behaviour becomes obvious
THE NLRI
RD · 8 bytes
IPv4 prefix · 4 bytes
Label · 3 bytes
unique per VRF
the customer's own prefix
the VPN label
THE ATTRIBUTES THAT MATTER
Route targets (extended community, 8 bytes each): the only field any policy acts on.
Next hop: the advertising PE loopback — must be reachable through transport, or the route is unusable.
AS path / origin / MED: unchanged in meaning from IPv4 BGP; still the inter-AS tie-breakers.
Local preference: still the first real decision inside the AS, now applied to VPN routes.
The customer prefix is carried verbatim: no summarization and no rewriting happens in the core.
Where the label comes from and goes
Ingress PE: allocates a VPN label per VRF
(or per prefix) and advertises it with the route.
Egress PE: reads the label, chooses the VRF,
removes it, delivers the IP packet.
The core swaps only the transport label above it.
This is why P routers need no VPN routes at all.
The dependency nobody draws: MP-BGP is not self-sufficient. Its next hop lives in the transport layer, so if the LSP to the next hop breaks,
BGP keeps the route and the FIB drops it. Symptoms look like “BGP is flapping” while the actual fault is one IGP adjacency two hops away.
Reading order in a ticket: VPNv4 table (is the route there, with which RT and label) → next hop reachable through transport → LFIB for the transport label → VRF table (was it imported).
Each step rules out one of the four fields above; guessing skips all four.
